name: The Bunyip
description: A bellowing creature of the billabongs and swamps of south-eastern Australia
origin: Aboriginal Australian traditions, especially of the Wemba-Wemba and other south-eastern peoples

debut.title: Aboriginal Australian oral tradition
debut.era: oral tradition for thousands of years; first printed in 1845

legend: The bunyip lives in the billabongs, swamps and waterholes of south-eastern Australia, and the word itself comes from the Wemba-Wemba people of what is now Victoria, though many nations have their own name and their own story. Descriptions vary enormously between peoples and tellings: some give it a dog's face, some tusks, flippers or a long neck, and some describe only a terrible bellowing in the night. What most tellings share is a warning to respect dangerous water, and in Ngarrindjeri tradition the related mulyawonk carries a lesson against taking more fish than you need. British settlers heard the stories and reported their own sightings, and in 1847 a strange skull found on the Murrumbidgee was exhibited in the Australian Museum in Sydney as a bunyip's; experts soon identified it as the deformed skull of a foal or calf. Scientists have since wondered whether the stories carry a memory of Diprotodon and other giant marsupials that lived alongside the first Australians.

myths.claim: Everyone agrees what a bunyip looks like.
myths.explanation: Descriptions differ from nation to nation and even from telling to telling, from a seal-like animal to a long-necked beast with tusks.

myths.claim: A museum once exhibited a bunyip skull.
myths.explanation: The Australian Museum in Sydney showed a supposed bunyip skull in 1847. It was soon identified as a deformed foal or calf skull.

myths.claim: The bunyip may be a memory of extinct giant animals.
myths.explanation: The naturalist George Bennett suggested in 1871 that the stories recall megafauna such as Diprotodon, a wombat-like marsupial the size of a car.

myths.claim: The bunyip is a settler invention.
myths.explanation: Settlers borrowed the word and the fright, but the stories belong to Aboriginal peoples and were old long before 1845.

powers: A bellow that carries across the swamp
Dragging the unwary into deep water
Being whatever the last witness said it was
weaknesses: Respectful fishing, which gives it no cause
Sceptical scientists with a tape measure
legacy: Bunyip Bluegum, the koala hero of Norman Lindsay's The Magic Pudding (1918)
The Bunyip of Berkeley's Creek (1973) by Jenny Wagner and Ron Brooks, a classic Australian picture book
The bunyip of the animated film Dot and the Kangaroo (1977), who frightened a generation of Australian children
facts: The bunyip comes from Aboriginal Australian traditions, especially in the south-east
The word bunyip is from the Wemba-Wemba language of Victoria
It lives in billabongs, swamps and waterholes and is often heard rather than seen
Descriptions vary greatly between nations and tellings
The word first appeared in print in the Geelong Advertiser in 1845
A supposed bunyip skull was exhibited in Sydney in 1847 and turned out to be a deformed foal or calf

hostIntro: Tonight's guest lives at the bottom of a billabong, and nobody can agree on what it looks like, which is exactly how it likes it. Listen for the bellow, and stay well back from the water's edge.
